title: ChimneyClear
question: How do a kitchen chimney and gas hob work?
hook: A spark of 14,000 volts, a jet of gas that drags in its own air, and a hood that catches smoke it can barely suck. Take an Indian kitchen's gas stove and chimney apart in 3D and see why a good flame is blue.

explainer.title: Gas from a cylinder, smoke out through a duct
explainer.text: LPG waits as a liquid in a 14.2 kg cylinder at about 5 bar. A regulator lets it out at a gentle 29 millibar, a hose carries it to the stove, and a valve behind each knob feeds a brass burner. Above, a chimney's blower pulls smoky air through grease filters and out through a duct.

explainer.title: Why a good flame is blue
explainer.text: The gas shoots from a tiny injector into a mixing tube and drags air in with it, the Bunsen principle. With about half the air it needs premixed, the flame burns clean and blue at up to about 1,900 °C. Starved of air, unburnt carbon glows yellow as soot and the flame makes carbon monoxide.

explainer.title: Thousands of volts to light it, millivolts to keep it safe
explainer.text: The igniter needs about 14,000 volts to make a spark jump a 4 mm gap. On stoves with a flame-failure device, a thermocouple in the flame makes about 28 millivolts to power a magnet that holds the gas valve open. If the flame dies, the voltage falls and a spring shuts the gas off.

explainer.title: The chimney doesn't suck the smoke up
explainer.text: At the pan, 70 cm below the hood, a chimney's suction is only about 0.05 m/s. The smoke rises by itself in a hot plume at about 1 m/s. The hood has to be low and wide enough to swallow that plume before a draught pushes it out from under the edge.

explainer.title: Oil can't turn corners
explainer.text: A baffle filter forces the air to zig-zag. Air follows easily, but oil droplets are about 750 times denser, so they keep going straight and hit the steel, then drain into the oil collector. Droplets smaller than a few microns slip through.

explainer.title: The number on the box is not the air you get
explainer.text: Rated suction is measured with nothing in the way. The filter, a narrow duct, bends and a shut window all push back, so a 1,200 m³/h chimney often moves half to two thirds of that. Where the fan curve meets the duct's system curve is the airflow you really get.

concepts.def: Liquefied petroleum gas: mostly propane and butane, stored as a liquid under pressure in a cylinder.
The valve on the cylinder that lowers the gas pressure to a steady 29 millibar for the stove.
Air mixed with the gas inside the burner before it reaches the flame.
A fast jet of gas drags the surrounding air into a tube with it, premixing fuel and air.
A poisonous, invisible gas made when fuel burns without enough oxygen.
Two different metals joined at a tip that make a small voltage when the tip is heated.
A thermocouple and magnet valve that shut off the gas if the flame goes out.
Catching particles by turning the air so sharply that they cannot follow and hit a surface.
How much pressure a duct needs for each airflow. Where it meets the fan curve is the real airflow.
